sentences.text: The accident took place with the vehicle i.e. DTC Bus bearing registration No. DL-1PD-4052 driven by respondent no. 1, Deepak Kumar; owned by respondent no. 2, Ajay Kumar and insured with respondent no. 3, The Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd.

BRIEF FACTS OF THE CASE:
2. Based on the facts outlined in the DAR and the claim petition, it emerges that on receiving a call on 24.08.2021 vide DD no. 35A, HC Inderesh Kumar along with Ct. Suresh reached at the spot i.e.
near Metro Depot near Nirmal Hriday, Majnu Ka Tila, Delhi, where one DTC Bus bearing registration no. DL-1PD-4052 and one motorcycle bearing registration no. DL-6SBG-2670 were stationed in accidental condition.
Both the vehicles were taken into custody.
They got to know that the injured had been taken to Trauma Centre, Delhi.
After leaving Ct. Suresh, IO went to Trauma Centre, Delhi and collected the MLC no. 26026/21 of injured Abhishek Kumar.
IO recorded the statement of the injured.
Thereafter, IO returned to the spot.
On the basis of MLC and statement of the injured, offence u/s. 279/337 IPC was registered against the driver of the offending vehicle.
3. During investigation, IO prepared the site plan and deposited both the vehicles in malkhana.
IO gave the notice u/s. 41.A Cr.PC to the driver of the offending vehicle who produced the documents of the offending vehicle and submitted the same with the IO.
Thereafter, mechanical inspection of both the vehicles was got conducted.
Documents pertaining to the offending vehicle were got verified and were found to be correct.
The IO deposited the MLC of the injured in the hospital for final opinion and upon collection, the injury was shown as 'grievous' on the MLC of the petitioner

, therefore,
section 338 IPC was added.
On completion of investigation, charge sheet under section 279/338 IPC was filed against the driver of the offending vehicle and DAR was filed before this Tribunal on 24.12.2021.
4. Respondent no. 1 filed his written statement and Respondent no. 3 filed its reply.
Respondent nos. 1 and 2 stopped appearing and thus, they were proceeded ex-parte vide order dated 13.08.2024.
ISSUES FRAMED 5.

On the basis of the pleading of the parties, vide order dated 07.11.2023, this Tribunal had framed the following issues:
1) Whether the petitioner Abhishek Kumar suffered injuries in an accident that took place on 24.08.2021 at about 10:20 AM involving vehicle bearing registration no.
DL-1PD-4052 (Bus) driven by the Respondent no.1 rashly and negligently, owned by the respondent no. 2 and insured with the respondent no. 3?
OPP 2) Whether the petitioner is entitled for any compensation?
If so, to what amount and from whom?
3) Relief.

My findings are as under:-
Analysis:
9.

Before delving into the facts of the current case to decide the aforementioned issues, it is pertinent to highlight that it is firmly established in legal precedents that the proceedings conducted before the Claims Tribunal are in the nature of an inquiry.

Further, procedural approach adopted by an accident claims' tribunal mirrors that of a civil court (National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Smt.
Pushpa Rana & Ors. 2009 ACJ 287).

Pushpa Rana & Ors. 2009 ACJ 287)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In civil proceedings, the establishment of facts hinges on a preponderance of probabilities, rather than being bound by the strict rules of evidence or the higher standard of beyond reasonable doubt, as required in criminal cases.
The burden of proof in civil cases is lighter than in criminal cases, and the burden to decide claim petition under The Motor Vehicles Act is even lesser as compared to a civil litigation.

In Bimla Devi & Ors. v. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors (2009) 13 SC 530, it has been held by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India that negligence must be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view must be adopted in reaching a conclusion.

12. PW-1, Mr. Abhishek Kumar, has proved the factum of the accident.
He has led categorical evidence to prove the identity of the respondent no.1 and the registration number of the offending vehicle.

He testified that on 24.08.2021 at about 10:20 AM, he was on his motorcycle bearing no.
DL-6SBG-2670 and when he was crossing under the Wazirabad flyover metro depot for filling the petrol, then the bus no. DL-1PG-4052, which was coming from ISBT at a very high speed and in a zigzag manner driven by the respondent Deepak, hit his motorcycle due to which, he fell down on the road and sustained grievous injuries.
He further testified that the PCR came to the spot and got him admitted in Trauma Centre, Civil Lines, Delhi where he was treated vide MLC no. 26026/21.
It was mentioned on the MLC that "Pt brought to casualty C A/H/O RTA around Nirmal Hridya Around 10:30 AM on 24.10.21 U/O fit for statement.
13. Further, respondent nos. 1 and 2 neither filed their written statements nor led any evidence to prove that the alleged offending vehicle was not involved in the present accident.

On the other hand,
PW-1 has unequivocally testified that respondent was driving the offending vehicle/ bus bearing registration no. DL-1PD-4052, at a very high speed, rashly and negligently without caring for the traffic rules which led to the accident in question.
The deposition of PW-1 as to the manner of the accident and the driving of the offending vehicle in a rash and negligent manner by the respondent remained uncontroverted and uncontradicted.
14. Moreover, the petitioner had no prior acquaintance with the respondent before the accident, and it is undisputed that there existed no pre-existing animosity between them.
Therefore, it defies every logic as to why the petitioner would falsely implicate the respondent if he was not the one driving the offending vehicle.
PW-1 has emphatically testified that the respondent was driving the offending vehicle rashly and negligently, resulting in the accident that caused grievous injuries to the petitioner.

The respondent no.1, who was the driver of the vehicle, would have been the most crucial witness capable of refuting the petitioner's allegations of the occurrence of the accident and rash and negligent driving.
However, he did not step into the witness box.
Thus, adverse inference is drawn against the respondent.
In this regard, reliance is placed on the judgments of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in the cases of Teja Singh Vs Suman & Ors., MAC.

sentences.text: No convincing material has been brought on record by the respondent to show that no accident took place or that the respondent was not rash and negligent while driving the offending vehicle.

15. It is also settled law that the petitioner cannot be expected to prove the accident to the hilt and the principle of res ipse loquitor should apply which means that the "accident speaks for itself".
Thus

, once it has been established in DAR and chargesheet that the accident had taken place, the burden shifts on the respondent to prove that he was not responsible for the accident which the respondent has clearly failed to discharge.
Thus, the factum of accident and the identity of the respondent as driver of the offending vehicle stands established.

Therefore, from the testimony of PW-1 and entire record, it stands proved that the respondent acted in a rash and negligent manner while driving his vehicle due to which the petitioner suffered grievous injuries.
16. Furthermore, in view of filing of DAR containing the charge-sheet for the offences u/s 279/338 IPC and other relevant documents against the respondent

and in terms of the judgment in the case of National Insurance Co. Vs. Pushpa Rana & Ors. 2009 ACJ 287 Delhi, the respondent no. 1 Deepak Kumar is held to be negligent on the basis of preponderance of probability.

sentences.text: Further, it is also clear from the DAR that the offending vehicle was owned by respondent no. 2, Ajay Kumar and insured with respondent no. 3, Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. vide policy no. 215100/31/2021/2018 for the period 24.03.21 till 23.03.22.
The factum of the said policy is admitted by respondent no. 3.
Contributory negligence:
Counsel for respondent no. 3 had argued that the petitioner/ injured was riding his motorcycle on the wrong side of the road and therefore, he was also negligent and contributed towards the accident.

He further argued that the IO had filed a kalandra u/s 119/177 MV Act for driving on the wrong side against the petitioner/ injured Abhishek which proves that he was riding his motorcycle on the wrong side of the road.

Ld. Counsel for the petitioner/ injured did not controvert this argument and therefore, keeping in view the kalandra filed by the IO, it is held that the petitioner/ injured was also negligent and contributed to the accident as he was driving on the wrong side of the road.
His negligence is fixed at 20%.

The injury:
18.
The petitioner (PW-1) testified that due to the accident, he sustained grievous injuries.
The petitioner asserted that upon the accident, he was taken to Sushruta Trauma Centre where he was treated vide MLC no. 26026/21 dated 24.08.2021.
It was recorded that the alleged history is road traffic accident and that the nature of injury suffered by the petitioner was opined to be grievous.

19. From the above deposition and in totality of the circumstances, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the petitioner has been able to bring on record sufficient facts so as to prove at the scales of preponderance of probabilities that the accident in question Abhishek Kumar (I) ... vs Deepak Kumar (Oriental Ins. Issue no. 2:
Whether the petitioner is entitled for compensation?
If so, to what amount and from whom?
The onus of proving the above issue was upon the petitioner/injured.

It has already been concluded in the preceding paragraphs while deciding the issue no.1,
that the petitioner had suffered grievous injury in the said accident.
21. The petitioner is certainly entitled for compensation in view of decision of the discussion on the above issues.

Before proceeding further to decide the present issue,
it would be apposite to encapsulate the law laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its guiding lamp post judgment for ascertaining just compensation in road vehicular injury cases.

In the case of Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Ors. (2011) 1 SCC 34, Hon'ble Supreme Court held as under:
"General principles relating to compensation in injury cases 4.

entities.text: Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Ors. (2011) 1 SCC 34
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The provision of The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (`Act' for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The Court or tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

(See C. K. Subramonia Iyer vs. T. Kunhikuttan Nair - AIR 1970 SC 376, R. D.
Hattangadi Vs. Pest Control (India) Ltd. - 1995 (1) SCC 551 and Baker vs. Willoughby - 1970 AC 467).

5. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following :
Pecuniary damages (Special Damages)
Abhishek Kumar (I) ... vs Deepak Kumar (Oriental Ins. Co. ) on 8 January, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/197884628/
7 (i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising :
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non-pecuniary damages (General Damages)
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage).
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).

In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i),
(ii)(a) and (iv).
22.

In view of the above law laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, in injury cases, award needs to be passed only under heads of medical expenses, loss of earning during treatment period and damages for pain, suffering and trauma.

This is a case where the petitioner has suffered grievous injuries, hence, this Tribunal now proceeds further step by step to decide the compensation/award under different heads applicable to the present matter in light of above preposition.

Loss of income:
26. Coming to the aspect of loss of income, the petitioner has claimed he was doing a private job as Assistant at Medical Store, D- Block Market, Defence Colony, Delhi and was earning Rs. 23,000/-
per month.
He has also stated that due to the accident in question he could not work for 12 months and suffered complete loss of earnings during that period.

However, the petitioner has not filed any document to show that he used to work as an Assistant at a medical store or that he was earning Rs.
23,000/- per month.
Thus, the income of the petitioner will have to be assessed as per the minimum wages.
The petitioner has filed on record his Aadhar card bearing no. 3221 4919 6825 as per which he was a resident of Delhi.
He has also filed his 10 th class certificate which shows that he was a matriculate.

Therefore, in the absence of proof of employment and income and considering his address to be of Delhi, the minimum wages for a matriculate prevalent in Delhi at the time of the accident (on 24.08.2021) i.e. Rs. 19,291/- is taken as the income of the petitioner/ injured Abhishek Kumar.
Therefore, it is held that the monthly income of the petitioner/ injured Abhishek Kumar at the time of the accident i.e. on 24.08.2021 was Rs. 19,291/-.
Further, the petitioner has claimed that he could not go to work for 12 months, however, he has not filed any document to prove the same.
Thus, keeping in view the nature of injuries sustained by the petitioner, it is held that the petitioner shall be entitled to the Loss of Income for 04 months i.e. Rs. 19,291/- x 4 = Rs. 77,164/-.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Further, procedural approach adopted by an accident claims' tribunal mirrors that of a civil court (National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Smt.
Pushpa Rana & Ors. 2009 ACJ 287).
In civil proceedings, the establishment of facts hinges on a preponderance of probabilities, rather than being bound by the strict rules of evidence or the higher standard of beyond reasonable doubt, as required in criminal cases.
The burden of proof in civil cases is lighter than in criminal cases, and the burden to decide claim petition under The Motor Vehicles Act is even lesser as compared to a civil litigation.
In Bimla Devi & Ors. v. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors (2009) 13 SC 530, it has been held by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India that negligence must be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view must be adopted in reaching a conclusion.
The deposition of PW-1 as to the manner of the accident and the driving of the offending vehicle in a rash and negligent manner by the respondent remained uncontroverted and uncontradicted.
14. Moreover, the petitioner had no prior acquaintance with the respondent before the accident, and it is undisputed that there existed no pre-existing animosity between them.
Therefore, it defies every logic as to why the petitioner would falsely implicate the respondent if he was not the one driving the offending vehicle.
PW-1 has emphatically testified that the respondent was driving the offending vehicle rashly and negligently, resulting in the accident that caused grievous injuries to the petitioner.
The respondent no.1, who was the driver of the vehicle, would have been the most crucial witness capable of refuting the petitioner's allegations of the occurrence of the accident and rash and negligent driving.
However, he did not step into the witness box.
Thus, adverse inference is drawn against the respondent.
28108/2017, titled as Reliance General Insurance Company Ltd. Vs Mona & Ors., date of decision 15.10.2019, which had relied upon the judgment in the case of Cholamandalam Insurance Co. Ltd.
Abhishek Kumar (I) ... vs Deepak Kumar (Oriental Ins. Co. ) on 8 January, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/197884628/
5 Vs Kamlesh 2009(3) AD Delhi 310.
, once it has been established in DAR and chargesheet that the accident had taken place, the burden shifts on the respondent to prove that he was not responsible for the accident which the respondent has clearly failed to discharge.
Thus, the factum of accident and the identity of the respondent as driver of the offending vehicle stands established.
Therefore, from the testimony of PW-1 and entire record, it stands proved that the respondent acted in a rash and negligent manner while driving his vehicle due to which the petitioner suffered grievous injuries.
16. Furthermore, in view of filing of DAR containing the charge-sheet for the offences u/s 279/338 IPC and other relevant documents against the respondent
and in terms of the judgment in the case of National Insurance Co. Vs. Pushpa Rana & Ors. 2009 ACJ 287 Delhi, the respondent no. 1 Deepak Kumar is held to be negligent on the basis of preponderance of probability.
In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i),
(ii)(a) and (iv).
